title: Session-aware slimline tokenizer: prefill microbatching and ASCII fast-path
creator: Marcus Chen
description: Reduce prefill-side CPU and latency overhead for short, high-QPS prompts by introducing a session-aware slimline tokenizer that applies an ASCII fast-path, lightweight normalization skipping, and microbatch aggregation hints to the serving runtime. This ticket covers design, microbenchmarks, a feature-flag rollout, and telemetry to validate end-to-end impact on tokenization CPU and downstream kernel warmup behavior.
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end median prefill latency for 0-64 token prompts reduced by >= 25% on p3-like instances compared to baseline (measured in perf harness)
CPU utilization for tokenization worker threads reduced by >= 20% under synthetic short-prompt load
No change in tokenization correctness for inputs that require full Unicode normalization (we fall back to standard pipeline)
Feature gated with server-side flag + clear telemetry; rollout plan documented and validated in staging
Corresponding GitHub PR passes CI and performance regression checks; PR link added to ticket
design_notes: Motivation: many hot paths are dominated by simple ASCII prompts (code, CLI, short chat), where full UTF-8 normalization and expensive regex-based cleaning are unnecessary

Core idea: a fast pre-check that classifies input as ASCII-simple, ASCII-with-escapes, or complex. ASCII-simple uses a slim pipeline: minimal normalization, single-pass byte->token mapping, and hinting to runtime that KV cache reuse is likely (session affinity)
Microbatching: aggregate prefill requests for the same session within a 2-5ms window to amortize tokenization overhead when bursty clients send multiple small prompts

Integration with kernel selection: expose per-request metadata (expected sequence length distribution, session affinity) so the serving runtime can pre-warm attention kernels and select quantized kernels optimized for short sequences
Fallbacks: if classification is uncertain or normalization required, route to existing full tokenizer implementation and record telemetry to refine heuristics
Determinism: ensure slimline tokenizer produces identical token IDs for ASCII inputs compared to full tokenizer; add unit tests for edge cases (emoji, non-breaking spaces)
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (Spike, 2 days): implement ASCII classifier and microbench synthetic harness to measure baseline CPU/latency
Phase 2 (Core work, 6 days): implement slimline tokenizer module, session microbatch aggregator, and lightweight normalization skipping. Add feature flag and server config toggles
Phase 3 (Runtime integration, 4 days): wire metadata into request routing so kernel selection can use hints; add pre-warm hook for attention kernels when aggregated prefill indicates low-latency path
Phase 4 (Testing & rollout, 3 days): unit + integration tests, canary rollout behind feature flag, monitor telemetry, iterate on heuristics
Expected total: 15 working days (estimation includes reviews and small follow-ups)
risks: Heuristic misclassification could under-tokenize or change token IDs if not perfectly aligned with full tokenizer — mitigated by deterministic mapping tests and immediate fallback on mismatch
Microbatching introduces small added latency for single-shot requests if window too long — will cap window to 2ms in initial rollout and tune from telemetry

Runtime integration adds new metadata surface; incorrect hints could lead to suboptimal kernel selection (warmups for wrong sequence lengths). Mitigation: conservative default hints and opt-in rollout
Observability gaps: need token-level breakdowns in Console to confirm savings; will add temporary dashboards during rollout
